summary: One of a series of surveys by David Smallberg checking which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP. This edition tested hosts in January 1983. Replaced by RFC 839.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on the door of every computer on the list to see which ones answered. This is the result for one week.

subtitle: A survey of TCP support on Internet hosts in January 1983.

tldr.problem: Early in the internet's history, there was no centralized way to know which machines were running TCP and what services they supported.
tldr.mechanism: David Smallberg systematically tested 323 hosts from the NIC hostname table by trying to connect to Telnet, FTP, and SMTP services over TCP, recording whether each connection was accepted, refused, unreachable, or failed.
tldr.outcome: Out of 323 hosts tested in January 1983, 172 accepted Telnet, 159 accepted FTP, and 154 accepted SMTP. The results show rapid growth in TCP adoption but also that some machines had stale hostname table entries.

today: RFC 838 was obsoleted by RFC 839, which updated the survey one week later in January 1983. While the RFC itself is now historical, it provides an invaluable snapshot of early TCP deployment and demonstrates how quickly the network was evolving at that time.

sections.title: The Survey
sections.content:
RFC 838 is the first in a series of surveys by David Smallberg documenting which computers on the early Internet actually supported TCP. From 12 January to 20 January 1983, Smallberg tested 323 hosts listed in the NIC hostname table by attempting to connect to three different services: Telnet, FTP, and SMTP.

Each host was tested for its ability to handle connections on the standard ports for these services. The survey reveals the practical state of TCP deployment in the early internet, which often differed from what the hostname table claimed.
sections.eli5: In January 1983, someone tested 323 computers by knocking on their door and asking to play a game. He recorded which ones answered and which ones didn't.

sections.title: How the Tests Were Run
sections.content:
Smallberg based his test list on the NIC hostname table as of 31 December 1982. The initial tests ran from 12 January at ~12:01 pm to 18 January at ~10:10 pm PST. Hosts that were dead, refused the connection, or were unreachable were retried on 19 January and 20 January to improve accuracy.

For each host, the survey recorded whether the host claimed to support each service (based on the hostname table flags: T = tcp, t = tcp/telnet, f = tcp/ftp, s = tcp/smtp) and whether the actual test succeeded, was refused, was unreachable, or found the host dead.
sections.eli5: The test list came from a book of computer names. He tried each one, and if he didn't reach it the first time, he tried again the next day.

sections.title: The Results
sections.content:
Of 323 hosts tested, 172 accepted Telnet connections, while 147 hosts claimed to support Telnet in the table. 159 accepted FTP connections out of 120 claiming FTP support. 154 accepted SMTP connections from 110 claiming SMTP. The gap between claims and reality shows that the hostname table was often out of date or inaccurate.

Additionally, 66 hosts were found to be dead (completely unresponsive), 11 were unreachable, and many had no TCP support at all. Among the hosts that did accept connections, some went further: a few FTP implementations allowed the standard test user 'anonymous' with password 'guest'.
sections.eli5: Out of 323 computers, 172 answered for Telnet, 159 for file transfers, and 154 for mail. But 66 of them didn't answer at all, which meant they were probably turned off or broken.

sections.title: What It Shows
sections.content:
The survey demonstrates that in January 1983, TCP was still being deployed at a rapid pace across the Internet. However, it also shows that not all computers on the network had adopted it yet, and that the central registry of hostnames was lagging behind reality. Many hosts were either dead or obsolete entries in the table.

The data suggests that Telnet was the most widely deployed TCP service, with 104 out of 147 Telnet-claiming hosts actually accepting connections. This early snapshot is valuable because it captures the state of the network in a pre-WWW era when TCP was still finding its place in the Internet ecosystem.
sections.eli5: This shows that computers were starting to talk to each other, but not all of them. Some computers on the list didn't exist anymore or had old phone numbers written down.
